prompt_free_text:
Summary

This paper studies test-time adaptation for concept bottleneck models built on top of foundation model features. The authors argue that although recent CBM variants can approach the accuracy of standard feature-based classifiers on the source domain, they can fail badly under deployment-time distribution shifts. To address this, they propose CONDA, a three-stage source-free adaptation framework using only unlabeled target data: (i) Concept Score Alignment (CSA), which adapts concept vectors to align target concept-score distributions to source class-conditional Gaussian statistics; (ii) Linear Probing Adaptation (LPA), which updates the concept-to-label linear layer using pseudo-labels; and (iii) Residual Concept Bottleneck (RCB), which adds new residual concepts and a residual classifier branch to compensate for incomplete concept sets. Experiments on CIFAR10/100-C, Waterbirds, MetaShift, and Camelyon17 with several CBM construction methods suggest substantial gains over unadapted CBMs, often bringing performance closer to non-interpretable zero-shot or linear-probe baselines.

Overall assessment

I think the paper addresses an interesting and timely problem: how to preserve interpretability benefits of concept bottlenecks while maintaining performance under distribution shift in foundation-model pipelines. The problem formulation is relevant, and the empirical results are generally strong. The decomposition into different failure modes and corresponding adaptation modules is intuitive and useful. The paper is also well motivated by the observation that CBMs are not automatically robust simply because they operate on concepts.

That said, I have several concerns about the technical framing, the strength of some claims, and the evaluation methodology. In particular, the theoretical formalization of shifts is somewhat idealized and not tightly connected to the actual algorithm; the adaptation relies heavily on pseudo-label quality and source-side stored statistics; and the interpretability claims around residual concepts are suggestive but not yet fully convincing. I view the paper as promising and likely worthy of discussion, but it would benefit from clarifications and some additional experiments.

Strengths

1. Important problem setting
The paper tackles a meaningful gap between interpretability and robustness in FM-based pipelines. Test-time adaptation for CBMs is a natural and underexplored direction.

2. Clear high-level insight
The central observation is compelling: concept bottlenecks are not inherently robust under shift, and may even underperform direct feature-based prediction after deployment. This is a useful message for the community.

3. Modular method design
The three-part decomposition into CSA, LPA, and RCB is sensible. It is especially nice that the authors try to map different adaptation components to different failure modes.

4. Broad empirical coverage
The experiments span multiple datasets, multiple shift types, multiple backbones, and multiple CBM construction methods. This breadth strengthens the empirical case.

5. Strong empirical gains in many settings
The improvements on Waterbirds and MetaShift are particularly notable. The method appears effective at recovering substantial worst-group accuracy.

Weaknesses and concerns

1. Theoretical framing is not fully aligned with the practical setting
Section 2 introduces low-level shift as preserving concept-score distributions and concept-level shift as changing concept-score distributions while preserving prediction distributions. This taxonomy is neat, but in practice the whole point of the paper is that the deployed concept mapping often does not satisfy these assumptions. So the definitions are more descriptive than operational. Also, many real shifts will mix both effects, and the paper does not clearly explain how the framework behaves when the shift does not fit either category.

Relatedly, Definition 1 on completeness is very strong and somewhat abstract. It is not clear how this notion is estimated, tested, or used algorithmically beyond motivating the residual branch.

2. Dependence on source-side statistics is stronger than the “source-free” framing suggests
The method assumes access to class-conditional Gaussian statistics of source-domain concept scores, and also to a source-trained linear probe used in pseudo-labeling. This is a reasonable practical assumption, but it should be stated more explicitly as a requirement. In many source-free adaptation settings, retaining such sufficient statistics is acceptable, but it is not equivalent to having no source information beyond the model.

I would like to see a clearer discussion of:
- what exact source artifacts must be stored,
- how large these artifacts are relative to the model,
- whether covariance matrices are full or diagonal,
- how sensitive CSA is to estimation quality of these statistics.

3. Pseudo-labeling may be doing much of the work
The pseudo-labeling strategy uses an ensemble of zero-shot and linear-probe predictions from the FM, selecting the more confident one. This is a fairly strong teacher, and in some datasets the FM baselines are already very good. It raises the question of how much of the gain comes from the CBM adaptation itself versus simply distilling a stronger non-interpretable predictor into the CBM at test time.

This is especially relevant because LPA and RCB optimize cross-entropy directly on pseudo-labels. If the pseudo-label teacher is strong, then the method may largely be a target-domain distillation procedure. That is not necessarily a flaw, but it should be acknowledged and quantified.

A stronger evaluation would compare against:
- directly using the pseudo-label teacher itself as the deployed predictor,
- adapting a standard linear probe with the same pseudo-labels and optimization budget,
- a CBM adaptation variant using self-labels only,
- a variant using only zero-shot or only linear-probe pseudo-labels.

4. Some comparisons are incomplete or potentially unfair
The main table compares adapted CBMs to unadapted zero-shot and linear-probe baselines, but not to adapted non-interpretable baselines under the same source-free setting. Since the paper’s claim is partly that CONDA can align CBM performance with non-interpretable classification, the most relevant comparison would be against strong TTA methods applied to the linear probe or FM classifier.

Without such baselines, it is hard to know whether CONDA is competitive as an adaptation method, or whether any model with access to the same pseudo-labels and target batches would improve similarly.

5. Interpretability claims need stronger evidence
The paper argues that CONDA improves interpretability because concept-based explanations become better aligned with target data, and residual concepts correspond to meaningful notions like feathers, wings, and beak. This is plausible, but the evidence presented in the main paper is mostly anecdotal.

I would like more rigorous interpretability evaluation, for example:
- human evaluation of concept quality before/after adaptation,
- concept purity/coherence metrics,
- stability of concept semantics across runs,
- whether residual concepts are non-redundant and consistently interpretable,
- whether adaptation preserves faithfulness of explanations.

There is also a tension here: adapting concept vectors to optimize target performance may drift them away from their original semantics. The Frobenius penalty helps, but the paper does not really quantify semantic drift in the main branch.

6. Residual branch may weaken the CBM premise
The residual concept bottleneck is effectively adding learned latent directions plus a linear classifier. While this is practical, it risks turning the model into a partially unconstrained low-rank adapter rather than a purely interpretable concept bottleneck. The paper should discuss this tradeoff more directly.

In particular:
- Are residual concepts human-nameable consistently?
- How many residual concepts are needed before interpretability degrades?
- Does performance continue to improve as r increases, and if so, does the model simply recover a generic linear adapter?

7. Method details and notation issues
There are several places where the exposition could be tightened:
- Eq. (5) is referred to later as Eq. (3) in Section 3.2 / Algorithm references appear inconsistent.
- The Mahalanobis distance formula appears to have a parenthesis typo.
- The Gaussian assumption over concept scores is strong; some justification or empirical validation would help.
- It is unclear whether covariance matrices are regularized for invertibility, especially for high-dimensional concept spaces or small classes.
- The online adaptation protocol can be order-sensitive; I did not see enough discussion of robustness to batch order.

8. Mixed empirical picture on some datasets
The method does not uniformly help. For example, on CIFAR100 with the Yeh et al. CBM, adaptation reduces AVG and WG. On Camelyon17, adaptation can also hurt for some CBM variants. These failures are important and should be analyzed more deeply in the main text, not only framed as overall success.

The paper currently emphasizes positive cases, but the negative cases are scientifically interesting:
- Why does adaptation hurt stronger CBMs?
- Is pseudo-label noise the culprit?
- Does CSA overfit when the source concept bank is already robust?
- Is there a criterion for deciding which modules to activate?

Detailed comments and questions

1. Shift taxonomy
The distinction between “low-level” and “concept-level” shift is intuitive, but the formal definitions are too rigid. For example, Gaussian noise may change concept scores under a non-robust concept extractor, and background changes may also alter prediction distributions if labels are spuriously correlated. In practice, shifts are model-relative. I suggest reframing these as idealized reference cases rather than exhaustive categories.

2. Source statistics for CSA
Please clarify exactly how the source Gaussian statistics are computed and stored. Are they based on the original source concept bank only? If so, after concept vectors are updated, why is matching to the old Gaussian family still appropriate? Is there any whitening or covariance shrinkage?

3. Why optimize concept vectors directly?
Updating concept vectors changes semantics. Why not instead learn an affine calibration in concept-score space? That might preserve concept meanings better. A comparison to score-space adaptation would be informative.

4. Pseudo-label confidence selection
The rule “take the class predicted with higher confidence across zero-shot and linear probe” is simple, but confidence scales across these predictors may not be calibrated. Did the authors calibrate them? If not, this comparison may be unreliable.

5. Sequential adaptation order
The method always applies CSA, then LPA, then RCB. Did the authors test alternative orders or selective activation? Figure 3 suggests that not all components help on all shifts. This points to the possibility of a shift-aware controller or validation-free module selection.

6. Evaluation metrics
The paper uses AVG and WG, which are appropriate for spurious correlation benchmarks. For CIFAR-C and Camelyon17, standard accuracy might also be useful for comparison with prior TTA work.

7. Runtime and memory
Since the method is intended for deployment, runtime matters. The appendix may contain complexity analysis, but the main paper should summarize adaptation cost more concretely.

8. Comparison to prior residual CBM work
The residual branch resembles recent residual/incremental CBM ideas. The paper cites Shang et al. (2024) in references but does not discuss it in the main method section. The novelty relative to residual CBMs plus standard TTA should be clarified.

Suggestions for improvement

1. Add stronger adaptation baselines
At minimum, compare against:
- TTA on the linear probe using the same pseudo-labels,
- entropy-minimization or MEMO/TENT-style adaptation where applicable,
- a direct FM adaptation baseline under the same source-free setting.

2. Quantify pseudo-label dependence
Include ablations for:
- self-labeling only,
- zero-shot only,
- linear-probe only,
- oracle pseudo-labels if possible,
- pseudo-label accuracy versus final adapted accuracy.

3. Strengthen interpretability evaluation
Provide quantitative concept quality metrics and examples across multiple runs/datasets, not just Waterbirds.

4. Analyze failure cases
Discuss datasets/CBMs where CONDA hurts performance, and identify when each module should or should not be used.

5. Clarify source-free assumptions
Be explicit that the method requires source-trained auxiliary predictors and source concept-score statistics.

6. Improve presentation
Fix equation numbering inconsistencies, notation typos, and streamline the formalism so it more directly supports the algorithm.

Recommendation

Weak Accept / Borderline

Rationale

The paper addresses an important and novel problem and presents a practically useful method with strong empirical gains in several challenging settings. The idea of adapting concept bottlenecks at test time is interesting and likely to inspire follow-up work. However, the current version overstates some claims around source-freeness and interpretability, and it lacks the strongest adaptation baselines needed to fully establish competitiveness. If accepted, I would encourage the authors to revise the framing and strengthen the empirical analysis accordingly.

Confidence

3/5

I am reasonably confident in my assessment of the paper’s strengths and weaknesses, though some appendix details may address a subset of my concerns.

prompt_structured_json.summary: This paper studies test-time adaptation for concept bottleneck models (CBMs) built on top of foundation model features under distribution shift. The authors identify three failure modes for deployed CBMs—non-robust concept mappings under low-level shifts, non-robust concept-to-label classifiers under concept-level shifts, and incomplete concept sets—and propose CONDA, a three-stage source-free adaptation framework using only unlabeled target data. CONDA performs concept-score alignment (CSA) by adapting concept vectors to match source class-conditional concept statistics, linear probing adaptation (LPA) by updating the concept-to-label layer with pseudo-labels, and a residual concept bottleneck (RCB) that adds new concepts to compensate for incompleteness. Experiments on CIFAR10/100-C, Waterbirds, Metashift, and Camelyon17 with several CBM constructions show substantial gains over unadapted CBMs, often bringing performance closer to non-interpretable baselines and sometimes improving worst-group accuracy markedly.
strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: adapting interpretable concept bottleneck pipelines, rather than only black-box classifiers, under test-time distribution shift.
Clear decomposition of failure modes into concept misalignment, classifier mismatch, and concept incompleteness, which motivates the three components of the method.
Method is modular and practically relevant in the source-free unlabeled target setting, assuming only access to the pretrained FM, CBM parameters, and source concept statistics.
Empirical evaluation spans multiple datasets, shift types, FM backbones, and CBM construction methods, which strengthens the claim of broad applicability.

Results show large improvements over unadapted CBMs, especially on concept-level shifts such as Waterbirds and Metashift, and often improve worst-group accuracy, which is particularly meaningful for robustness.
Ablation-style discussion of CSA/LPA/RCB roles is insightful and aligns the components with different shift types.
The residual concept branch is a sensible mechanism for handling incomplete concept banks and connects interpretability with adaptation.
The paper includes some interpretability analysis showing how adapted and residual concepts change in intuitive ways after adaptation.
weaknesses: The theoretical formalization of shift types and completeness is somewhat idealized and not tightly connected to the optimization objectives or guarantees; it mainly serves as intuition rather than rigorous support.
The method depends heavily on pseudo-label quality from zero-shot/linear-probe ensembles, but there is limited analysis of failure cases when these pseudo-labels are poor or biased.
CSA assumes access to source class-conditional Gaussian statistics in concept space; this is weaker than source data access but still a nontrivial requirement that may limit applicability.
The Gaussian assumption for class-conditional concept distributions and Mahalanobis-based alignment may be too restrictive, especially for multimodal concept distributions.

Some empirical results are mixed: CONDA can hurt performance for stronger CBMs on certain low-level shifts (e.g., CIFAR100 and Camelyon17 with Yeh et al.), suggesting the method is not uniformly beneficial.

Interpretability claims for residual concepts rely partly on automated annotation and qualitative examples; there is limited quantitative evaluation of concept quality, faithfulness, or human usefulness after adaptation.
The online adaptation protocol may be sensitive to batch order and error accumulation, but robustness to ordering or streaming conditions is not clearly analyzed.

Comparisons are mostly against unadapted CBMs and non-interpretable baselines; stronger baselines from the broader TTA literature adapted to the same FM+head setting would better isolate the contribution.
soundness_issues: The central methodological choices are plausible, but the paper provides no formal guarantees that CSA alignment using pseudo-labels and Gaussian source statistics improves target risk; the justification is heuristic.

The definition of low-level shift as preserving concept-score distributions and concept-level shift as preserving prediction distributions is conceptually neat but may not reflect real datasets cleanly; empirical datasets likely violate these assumptions.

Pseudo-labels are generated using models trained with source supervision (linear probe) and zero-shot prompts; if these are inaccurate under shift, all three adaptation stages may reinforce errors. The paper acknowledges this but does not fully characterize the risk.

The residual branch improves accuracy but may weaken interpretability because newly learned concepts are optimized primarily for predictive utility; the coherence/similarity regularizers help, but evidence of faithful concept semantics is limited.

Because source-domain concept statistics are precomputed and retained, the method is not entirely source-agnostic in an information-theoretic sense; this should be viewed as source-free adaptation with stored sufficient statistics rather than fully source-independent adaptation.

Some claims in the introduction/abstract are stronger than the evidence supports, particularly around 'better aligned' interpretations and matching non-interpretable classification across settings, since several results remain below the best black-box baselines.
